plain: ChatGPT is an app from the company OpenAI where you write in English what you need and it hands you back text: an email, a table, a work plan, or the instructions that make your website run. Think of a brilliant intern, tireless but with a terrible memory: it solves in thirty seconds what would cost you an afternoon, but every time you start a new conversation it shows up remembering nothing, and you have to explain again what you're working on. It also talks and listens through your phone's speaker, looks at photos you show it, and has a side workspace where a piece of text or a set of instructions stays put while the two of you correct it together. It knows nothing about your business until you tell it, and you have to tell it in writing.

account.free: Yes, there's a free plan and it's enough to do the whole course. With a free account you get unlimited conversations with the fast model (the brain), a limited number of daily messages with the model that stops to think, a handful of daily file and image uploads, voice mode with a daily cap, Canvas, and Projects. When you use up a cap it doesn't charge you: it drops you straight to the small model and tells you what time it resets. The paid plan is called ChatGPT Plus: list price is 20 dollars a month, and with Spanish VAT it comes out to around 23 EUR a month. The exact amount shows on the payment screen before you confirm; don't trust this figure without checking there. Plus gives you much higher limits, early access to new features, and fewer cutoffs at peak times. Above that is ChatGPT Pro, around 200 dollars a month (close to 240 EUR), which you don't need anywhere near for what this course covers. OpenAI has also been testing a cheaper mid-tier plan called Go, with availability varying by country: if it shows up on your plans screen, check it there — don't take my word on the price.
steps: Go to chatgpt.com and click "Sign up", top right. It lets you in with Google, Microsoft, Apple, or a new email and password. Pick the method you'll always use and make a note of it: a lot of people create the account with Google, then months later log in with email and password, find no conversations, and think everything got deleted. They're two different accounts.

It asks for your name, date of birth, and, almost always, a phone number it sends a six-digit code to. It's a normal verification, not a payment, and it doesn't ask for a card for the free plan. If the message doesn't arrive within two minutes, click "Resend code" before retyping the number.

At the very top, above the conversation, there's a dropdown with the model's name. That's where you choose the brain that answers you: there's an automatic option, a fast one, and one that stops to think for a few seconds before replying. The commercial names change every few months; what doesn't change is that difference. For writing code, always pick the one that thinks.

Click your photo or initial, bottom left, and go into "Settings", then "Personalization", then "Custom instructions". These are four text boxes that ChatGPT reads before every response, in all your conversations. It's the setting that changes the quality of what you get the most, and almost nobody touches it. The ready-to-paste template is further below.
Decide what it remembers about you

On that same "Personalization" screen there are two toggles: "Reference saved memories" and "Reference chat history". Turned on, ChatGPT saves data about you and reuses it in future conversations. Next to them is "Manage memories", where you see the full list and delete entries one by one. Turn them on if you're working on your own things; turn them off if you're going to paste client data.

In "Settings" there's a "Data controls" section with a toggle like "Improve the model for everyone". Turned on, your conversations can be used to train future versions. Turn it off before pasting anything from a client. Right there is also "Export data", which emails you a file with your entire history, and account deletion, which is genuinely irreversible.

In the left sidebar click "Projects" and then the "+" sign or "New project". A project is a folder with its own memory: it saves that topic's conversations, the files you upload, and a set of fixed instructions that apply only inside it. Everything you build during the course lives inside a project, not in loose conversations.
account.warning: Three warnings, worst to least. One: what you paste leaves your computer. Never paste passwords, API keys (the very long password one program uses to talk to another), card numbers, or a client's tax ID. If ChatGPT hands you back code with a key inside it, consider that key burned and change it. Two: deleting a conversation can't be undone. Ctrl + Shift + Backspace deletes the one you have open, and the warning is a small box you accept without reading; if that held the only copy of your code, it's gone. Always keep your files on your computer, never only in the chat history. Three: the Plus plan auto-renews every month until you cancel it by hand in "Settings" then "Subscription", and the month already started isn't refunded.

first: Open "Settings", then "Personalization" and "Custom instructions", and paste this document's template, changing what's in brackets. Ten minutes that save you a hundred corrections.

Create a project in the sidebar, name it after what you're going to build, and paste the project instructions from template 2 inside it. From here on, all your conversations on that topic go inside it.

Inside the project, switch the model to the one that thinks, and write: "Before writing any code, ask me ten numbered questions about what I want to build." Answer all ten. You're no longer talking to a stranger.

Ask for the first version as a single file. When the code appears, click the "Copy" button in the corner of the block, open Notepad, and save it as index.html with "Save As" and file type "All files". Double-click the file: it opens in your browser. That's already your website.

Ask for a small, specific change ("make the title bigger and the background cream") and check that it hands you the whole file back, not a fragment. If it trims it, that's when to learn to demand the full thing: that fight is 80% of the course.
shortcuts: Ctrl + Shift + O (Cmd + Shift + O on Mac)
Opens a new conversation without touching the mouse. You'll use this every day, because the golden rule is one task, one conversation: when you finish the contact section, new chat for the form.
Shift + Esc
Sends the cursor to the text box from anywhere on the page. Sounds trivial until you've spent half an hour reading a long answer and don't want to hunt for the box with the mouse.
Ctrl + /
Shows the full shortcut list for your version. If something in this table doesn't work because OpenAI has changed it, this is the up-to-date truth.
Ctrl + Shift + I
Opens custom instructions instantly. You'll tweak these more than you think: every time ChatGPT does something annoying twice, that quirk gets fixed here, not by repeating yourself in every message.
Ctrl + Shift + ;
Copies the last code block in the conversation. It's the star shortcut of vibecoding: don't hunt for the "Copy" button, hit this and paste it into your file.
Ctrl + Shift + C
Copies the entire last response, text and explanation included. For when what you want to save isn't the code but the step-by-step plan.
Shift + Enter
Line break without sending the message. Essential for writing a ten-line request without it firing off mid-sentence.
Ctrl + Shift + Backspace
Deletes the open conversation. I'm listing it here so you recognize it if you hit it by accident: a confirmation box pops up and, if you accept, there's no trash can and no going back.
Alt + Space (Windows desktop app; on Mac it's usually Option + Space)

Opens a small floating ChatGPT window over whatever you're doing, without switching programs. Handy for asking a question with the error right in front of you. It can be changed in the app's settings, and if another program has already claimed that combination, it won't respond.
Microphone button vs. the wave button, to the right of the text box

They're two different things. The microphone is dictation: you speak, it writes it down, and you decide when to send. The wave is voice mode: it turns into a real spoken conversation, it answers out loud, and you can interrupt it. To fire off a long request while driving or cooking, use the microphone.
daily: One task, one conversation. As soon as you switch topics, start a new chat. Very long conversations fill up and ChatGPT starts forgetting the beginning without telling you: it hands you back code that no longer matches what you already have.

Always demand the complete file. The phrase that works is: "Give me the whole file, from the first line to the last, no ellipses and no comments like 'the rest stays the same'." If you don't ask for it, it trims it, you paste the fragment, and your site goes blank.
Take a screenshot and drag it into the text box. ChatGPT sees images. When something looks off, crooked, or out of place, a screenshot is worth more than two paragraphs describing it.

Work in Canvas for what you're editing, and in the chat for what you're just asking about. A piece of text or a file you're going to touch twenty times lives in Canvas, where it stays put and gets corrected piece by piece. A one-off question goes in the chat and gets forgotten.

Choose the thinking model for anything hard. The fast option is fine for rewriting an email. For code, for crunching numbers, or for deciding how to put something together, switch the dropdown to the one that stops to think, even if it takes thirty seconds.

Close the session with a status report. Before you leave, ask it to summarize in one block what exists, what works, what's broken, and what the next step is. Paste that into your PROJECT file, and tomorrow start the new chat by pasting it back in.

templates.name: Custom instructions for vibecoding
templates.what: The text that gets pasted into the four "Custom instructions" boxes. It tells ChatGPT, once and for all your conversations, that you don't know how to code, that it should speak plain English, and that it must never trim your code. Useful for anyone who's going to build something by copying and pasting.
templates.how: Click your photo or initial bottom left, go into "Settings", then "Personalization", then "Custom instructions" (shortcut: Ctrl + Shift + I). You'll see four text boxes. Copy the block below, split each part into its box according to the titles marked with ===, replace what's in brackets with your own details, and click "Save". Close and open a new conversation so it starts applying: conversations already open don't pick up the change.
fill: [YOUR NAME]
What you want it to call you. Your first name is enough.
[YOUR TRADE]
What you actually do for a living. This changes its examples and comparisons entirely.
[WINDOWS 11 / MAC]
Your operating system. Without this it'll give you the other one's shortcuts and folder paths.
[CHROME / EDGE / SAFARI]
The browser you open your files with.
[DESCRIBE IT IN TWO SENTENCES]
What you're building right now. Update it whenever you switch projects.
[0 EUR / 10 EUR / 30 EUR]
The most you're willing to pay per month. Keeps it from suggesting 90 EUR services as if that were nothing.
templates.code:
=== FIELD 1: "What should ChatGPT call you?" ===
[YOUR NAME]

=== FIELD 2: "What do you do?" ===
I work in [YOUR TRADE: handmade ceramics / physiotherapy / wine sales]. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn. I build things by talking to you: I ask in plain English, you write the complete code, I copy it, paste it into a file, and open it. I use [WINDOWS 11 / MAC] and the browser [CHROME / EDGE / SAFARI].

=== FIELD 3: "What traits should ChatGPT have?" ===
Plain, direct English, short sentences. No introductions and no summaries at the end.
When you give me code: ALWAYS give me the entire file, from the first line to the last. Never write "the rest stays the same", "...", or "here goes your previous code". If the file is very long, warn me and split it into two consecutive messages, but don't trim it.
Before each code block, tell me in one line: which file this is, what it's called, and where I save it.
After each block, tell me how I check with my own eyes that it works.
If you're missing a detail, ask me. Don't make it up.
If something costs money or is irreversible, write it in capital letters before I do it.
Translate any technical term in parentheses the first time you use it.

=== FIELD 4: "Anything else ChatGPT should know" ===
My current project: [DESCRIBE IT IN TWO SENTENCES].
Tools I already use: [NONE / NOTEPAD / VS CODE / NETLIFY].
Maximum monthly budget: [0 EUR / 10 EUR / 30 EUR]. If a solution goes over that, suggest the free option even if it's worse.

templates.name: Project instructions for building a website or a shop
templates.what: The fixed rules that apply only inside one specific project. They're stricter and more specific than the custom ones: this is where the files that already exist go, what shouldn't be touched, and the spending limit. Useful for not repeating context in every new conversation within the same project.
templates.how: In the sidebar, open your project. In the project panel there's an instructions button that, depending on the version, shows up as "Instructions" or behind the three-dot icon. Paste the block below, fill in the brackets, and save. From then on, every conversation you open INSIDE the project already carries them. Update the CURRENT STATUS section every time you finish something: it's a living file, not decoration.
fill: WHAT WE'RE BUILDING
One specific sentence with what you want. "A pretty website" doesn't count; "a page with a gallery and a contact form" does.
CURRENT STATUS
The files you already have saved and the last thing you saw working with your own eyes.
What I want next
A single goal. One. If you list three, you'll get three half-solutions.
WHAT NOT TO TOUCH
What you already like and don't want changed on its own: colors, text, fonts.
templates.code:
WHAT WE'RE BUILDING
[A ONE-PAGE WEBSITE FOR MY CERAMICS STUDIO, WITH A PHOTO GALLERY AND A CONTACT FORM]

WHO I AM
I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn. I copy and paste what you give me. I have nothing installed besides the browser and Notepad.

FIXED RULES FOR THIS PROJECT
1. One file per message. Complete. No trims, no ellipses.
2. Mandatory header before the code: FILE NAME + FOLDER IT GOES IN.
3. No installing programs, terminals, or new accounts without telling me first and explaining why.
4. Only technology that works by double-clicking the file: plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No frameworks until I ask for them.
5. If something costs money, tell me the price in euros per month BEFORE proposing it.
6. Whenever you change something, tell me in one line what changed and how I'll see it on screen.
7. Plain, direct English, short sentences, no flourishes.

CURRENT STATUS
Files I already have: [index.html]
The last thing that worked: [THE PAGE DISPLAYS AND THE MENU SCROLLS TO EACH SECTION]
What I want next: [FOR THE FORM TO SEND ME AN EMAIL]

WHAT NOT TO TOUCH
[THE COLORS AND FONT ARE ALREADY DECIDED. DON'T CHANGE THEM WITHOUT ASKING.]

templates.name: PROJECT.md, the external memory ChatGPT doesn't have
templates.what: A text file that YOU keep on your computer with the real status of what you're building. It's the solution to the number one problem in vibecoding: the conversation fills up, it forgets, and you start from scratch every couple of days. With this, every new chat starts knowing everything with a single paste.
templates.how: Open Notepad, paste the block below, fill in the brackets, and save it as PROJECT.md in the same folder as your website (in "Save As", choose the type "All files", otherwise it turns into .txt). Every time you open a new conversation, drag the file into ChatGPT's text box or paste its contents before asking anything. When you finish the session, ask it "update PROJECT.md with what we did today", copy what it hands back, and overwrite the file.
fill: [NAME] and [DATE]
Your project's name and today's date, so you know if the file is stale.
Files that exist right now
The real list, with the folder they're in. If you lie here, ChatGPT will give you instructions for phantom files.
What ALREADY works
Only what you've seen with your own eyes on screen. Not what should work.
Decisions made
What's already settled, so it doesn't propose something different every week.
Things we already tried that failed
The section that saves the most time. Keeps it from sending you down the same dead end three times.

templates.name: Starter index.html for requesting changes in Canvas
templates.what: A complete, working single-piece web page: title, menu, three sections, cards, contact button, and a design that looks good on mobile. Nothing needs installing. Useful as a starting point so ChatGPT modifies something that already exists instead of inventing from scratch, which is when it works best.
templates.how: Copy the whole block. Open Notepad (or TextEdit on Mac, in plain-text mode), paste, and use "Save As" with the name index.html and type "All files". Save it in a new desktop folder called myweb. Double-click the file: it opens in your browser and that's already your page. Then, in ChatGPT, paste the content into a conversation and type "open this in Canvas". The side panel opens and from there you request changes in plain English; when it looks right, hit the "Copy" button at the top of the panel and overwrite your file.
fill: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
Shows up in the browser tab, in the big title, and in the footer.
[WHAT YOU DO, IN ONE SHORT SENTENCE]
The line under the title. Be specific: what you sell and to whom.
[SERVICE 1/2/3]
The three cards. If you only have two services, delete a whole card or ask ChatGPT to do it.
Your real prices. If you don't want to show them, ask it to swap the section for "free quote, no obligation".
[YOUREMAIL@EXAMPLE.COM]
Your email behind mailto:. Get this wrong and the button opens the mail app with a fake address, and you'll never notice.
--background, --ink, and --accent
The three colors. Change these lines and you change the whole page.

errors: "You've reached the maximum length for this conversation, but you can keep talking by starting a new chat."

The conversation is full. Every chat has a limit on how much text fits inside, and you've hit it. There's no point insisting. Before you leave, in the last message it still accepts, ask for the status report: what exists, what works, what's broken, and the next step. Copy that, open a new chat with Ctrl + Shift + O, and paste it in along with your current file. A warning sign worth recognizing beforehand: it starts giving you back code that contradicts what you already had. That means it's running out of room.
"Something went wrong. If this issue persists please contact us through our help center at help.openai.com."

The generic house error. It's almost always a passing server hiccup, not your fault. Order of things to try: click the regenerate icon under the response, reload the page with F5, try an incognito window, and if it persists, check status.openai.com to see if the service is down. Practical tip: if you were writing a very long message, copy it before reloading, because it sometimes gets lost.
"You've hit the Free plan limit for GPT-5." or "You've reached your limit for... Try again after 15:42."

You've used up the good model's quota on the free plan. It won't charge you anything. You can keep going with the small model, which is fine for quick questions but noticeably weaker for code. Two options: wait until the time it tells you, or move to Plus for about 23 EUR a month. Trick to stretch the free quota: don't spend messages from the good model on chatting, drafting emails, or asking trivial questions — save it for code.
"The message you submitted was too long, please reload the conversation and submit something shorter."

You pasted more at once than fits in one message. It usually happens when pasting a very long complete file. The good fix isn't splitting it by hand: upload the file with the "+" button and then "Add photos and files", instead of pasting the content directly. That way it reads it as a document and it doesn't take up space in the message.
"It seems there was an error while trying to access the file. Could you please re-upload it?" (it asks again for a file you uploaded twenty minutes ago)

The temporary workspace where ChatGPT had your file has reset. This happens on its own, from time or from inactivity. You haven't lost anything: the original is still on your computer. Upload it again and carry on. The underlying lesson: what you upload to ChatGPT is a disposable copy. The real version of your files lives in your folder, always.
Code with "// ... rest of the code stays the same" or "<!-- your previous content goes here -->" in the middle

It's not an error, it's the trap that costs the most hours. ChatGPT decided to save effort and gave you a fragment, not the file. If you paste that over yours, your site goes blank. How to spot it without knowing how to code: check the length. If yesterday's file had 150 lines and today's has 40, it's been trimmed. Fix it with one sentence: "Give me the COMPLETE file again, from the first line to the last, no ellipses and no comments referring to previous code." And prevent it by putting that in your custom instructions.
You save the file, double-click it, and the browser shows the code as plain text; or the file is called index.html.txt

Notepad saved it as plain text instead of a web page. Windows hides the extension so you don't see it. Fix: in Notepad, "File" then "Save As"; in the "Type" dropdown choose "All files" (*.*), type the full name index.html, and save. To see what's really happening, in File Explorer go to the "View" tab and check "File name extensions".
"I'm sorry, but I can't help with that." or the orange warning "This content may violate our usage policies."

It refused. Sometimes with reason, sometimes because a single word tripped the filter: this happens a lot with text about security, health, or money. Rephrase, explaining the real, legitimate context in one sentence ("I own this website and want to check that the form doesn't let spam through"). If it refuses twice to an honest request, open a new chat and phrase it differently: dragging a refusal along inside the same conversation tends to contaminate the following answers.

prompts.name: Start a project from scratch without it writing a line before understanding you
prompts.prompt: I want to build [WHAT YOU WANT: a one-page website for my ceramics studio / a shop with ten products / an assistant that answers my customers' questions]. Read this whole thing before answering. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: the deal is that I ask you for things in plain English, you write the complete code, and I copy it, paste it into a file, and open it. I work on [WINDOWS 11 / MAC], I use the [CHROME / EDGE / SAFARI] browser, and I have no programming software installed. My maximum budget is [0 / 10 / 30] EUR a month and I want it finished before [DATE]. Before writing a single line of code, ask me up to ten numbered questions about what I need, and don't give me any technical answer until I've answered all of them. Ask what actually changes the outcome: who's going to visit, from phone or computer, whether someone needs to be able to pay me, whether I have photos, whether I have a domain. Once I answer, give me back four things in this order. One: my project summarized in a single sentence, so I can confirm we understood each other. Two: the exact list of files we're going to create, with their name and the folder they go in. Three: the step-by-step plan, where each step ends with something I can see working on screen. And four: a section titled ASSUMPTIONS with everything you had to take for granted. If something I'm asking for is impossible, or costs more than my budget, tell me now and suggest the cheap alternative. Don't write any code yet.

prompts.name: Get the complete file and know where to put it
prompts.prompt: I need the file [FILE NAME: index.html] with this change: [THE CHANGE IN ONE SENTENCE: the top menu should stay fixed when scrolling and the background should be cream]. Delivery rules, no exceptions. First: give me the ENTIRE file, from the very first line to the last, exactly as it should be saved. Never write ellipses, or "the rest stays the same", or "keep your previous code here", and never give me just the part that changed. I don't know where a fragment fits in. If the file comes out too long for one message, warn me and split it into two consecutive, numbered messages, but without trimming anything. Second: before the code block, write one line saying what the file is called and which folder it goes in. Third: after the block, explain in two or three plain sentences what changed and how I check it with my own eyes by opening it in the browser; if I need to refresh with Ctrl + F5 to stop the browser from showing the old version, say so. Fourth: at the end of the message, tell me how many lines the file you just gave me has, so I can compare it to the one I already have and catch if you've trimmed it. Fifth: if making this change also requires touching another file, tell me before starting and wait for me to say yes. The context is the file I just pasted, and whatever already works doesn't get touched.

prompts.name: Debug a failure by pasting what you actually see
prompts.prompt: Something broke and I need to fix it. I'm giving you exact facts, not my own interpretations. What I did right before: [I PASTED THE FILE YOU GAVE ME AND SAVED IT]. What I expected to see: [THE PAGE WITH THE MENU ON TOP AND THE THREE CARDS]. What I'm actually seeing: [A BLANK SCREEN / TEXT WITH NO COLORS / THE BUTTON DOES NOTHING]. The literal error message, copied exactly: [PASTE THE EXACT TEXT HERE, OR WRITE "NO MESSAGE APPEARS"]. I'm also attaching a screenshot and the complete file I have saved right now, which is the one that rules: if what you gave me before and this one don't match, trust this one. Before giving me a fix, tell me in two plain sentences what you think the cause is, and give it a confidence percentage. If you're not at least 80% confident, don't give me the fix yet: tell me what you need to see and exactly how I get it, step by step, with the exact names of the buttons and menus I need to click on [WINDOWS 11 / MAC]. If you ask me to open the browser console, tell me which key to press and exactly where to look. When you do give me the fix, give me the complete file, not the loose patch, and add one line on how I confirm with my own eyes that it's fixed. And if we already tried this without success, say so and try a different route instead of repeating it.

prompts.name: Close the session with a status report that's useful tomorrow
prompts.prompt: Let's wrap up for today. This conversation is already very long and tomorrow I'll open a new one from scratch, so I need a status report to act as memory. Write it as a single block of text I can copy in full and save to my PROJECT.md file, with this content in this order. One: the project in one sentence, so a stranger could understand it. Two: the list of files that exist right now, with their exact name, the folder they're in, and one line saying what each does. Three: what ALREADY works, and only what we confirmed today by seeing it on screen, not what should work in theory. Four: what doesn't work yet, with the symptom exactly as it appears. Five: the decisions we've made that I don't want to revisit tomorrow, including colors, names, prices, and spending limit. Six: the paths we already tried that failed, with one line explaining why, so we don't repeat them. Seven: the next step, one single, specific one. And eight: the exact message, word for word, that I want to open tomorrow's new conversation with, so you pick up right here, assuming I'll attach this file and the current code. Write it in plain English, no untranslated jargon, no fluff. No congratulating me on progress: just the facts.

prompts.name: Ruthless reviewer before showing it to someone or paying for something
prompts.prompt: Switch roles. Up to now you've been the builder; now you're the reviewer with a chip on your shoulder, as if you were paid to find the flaw. I'm handing you [THE FILE / THE PROPOSAL YOU JUST GAVE ME] and here's what I'm about to do with it: [PUBLISH IT ON MY DOMAIN / SHOW IT TO A CLIENT / SIGN UP FOR THE SERVICE YOU'RE SUGGESTING]. Before I take that step, give me five short lists. One: what's going to break as soon as real people start using it, ranked by likelihood, with the specific symptom I'll see on screen. Two: where this could cost me money without my noticing — that is, subscriptions that auto-renew, services with a free tier that start charging once you cross a limit, domains that expire; give me the price in euros per month and tell me if I need to cancel by hand. Three: what here is irreversible, meaning if I click it, it can't be undone. Four: what other people's data this touches and what obligations that brings under [YOUR COUNTRY]'s laws; don't give me legal advice, just flag what I should check with someone. Five: what you assumed on your own that I never confirmed. Be specific and boring: no generic warnings like "review security". If one of the lists is empty, write EMPTY and don't pad it to look good. End with the single step you'd take first if this were yours.

words: Prompt (request)

What you write to it. It's not a search query, it's a request to someone who can't see your screen or know your business. "Build me a website" gets you something generic; "a page for my ceramics studio in Segovia, mobile-friendly, with a six-photo gallery and a button to write to me" gets you something you can actually use.
Model (the brain)

The specific version answering you, the one you pick in the dropdown at the top. There's a fast one, which answers instantly and works for writing, and one that stops to think for a few seconds and is the one you need for code and decisions. The commercial names change every few months; that difference doesn't.
Token (chunk)

The unit the machine splits text into to count it. A chunk is roughly three-quarters of a word. It matters because limits aren't measured in pages or messages, but in this: which is why a pasted code file uses up far more than a long question.
Context window (what fits)

How much text it can keep in mind at once within a conversation. When it fills up, it starts forgetting the beginning, and it does so silently, without warning you. This is why, by mid-afternoon, it hands you back code that contradicts what it gave you that morning.
Canvas (the workbench)

A panel that opens to the right with your text or code inside, where the content stays put instead of scrolling up with every message. You can select a single paragraph and ask for a change just there. It has version history and copy/download buttons.
Project

A folder inside ChatGPT that groups conversations, files, and instructions specific to one subject. Whatever you write in its instructions applies to every conversation inside it and to none outside it.
Custom instructions

Four text boxes in settings that ChatGPT reads before responding, always, in every conversation. This is where you fix its quirks once and for all, instead of repeating the same instruction every morning.
Memory

The habit of saving your data between conversations. It's toggled on and off in "Personalization", and reviewed and deleted item by item in "Manage memories". Convenient when you're working with your own things, awkward when handling client data.
Hallucination

When it makes something up with total confidence: a function that doesn't exist, a button that program doesn't have, a round price that sounds perfect. It doesn't warn you. That's why prices, dates, and menu names get double-checked by actually looking at the screen.
Vibecoding

Building programs by describing what you want in your own language while the machine writes the code. You decide what gets done and check whether it works; it types. It works surprisingly well for small, specific things, and falls apart when you ask for an entire system in one go.
matters: The conversation fills up and starts forgetting without telling you. There's no alarm at all: past a certain point, it simply hands you back code that no longer matches what you have, and you go crazy pasting things that break what worked. Ignore this and you lose whole afternoons and end up blaming the tool. The habit that prevents it costs two minutes: one task per conversation, a status report before closing, and a PROJECT.md file on your computer that you paste in when you start.

It trims your code on its own and you don't notice. It's the mistake that costs non-programmers the most hours, because "// rest stays the same" doesn't look like an error, it looks like a friendly note. You paste the file, your site goes blank, and you have no idea why. It's caught by comparing yesterday's file length to today's, it's prevented by demanding it in every request, and above all it's prevented in "Personalization": ten minutes writing your instructions there are worth more than a hundred loose corrections. Without them, ChatGPT treats you like a programmer, throws terminal commands at you, and assumes you have things installed. It's the highest-payoff setting in the whole app, and almost nobody opens it.

ChatGPT isn't talked to the same way as Claude or Gemini, and mixing them up costs you the day. ChatGPT is fast, summarizing, and very eager: it fills in gaps on its own without asking you and tends to give you the changed fragment instead of the whole file. With it you have to be bossy and repetitive: "complete file", "ask me if you're missing a detail", "don't assume anything". Claude, on the other hand, tends to write long, complete files without being asked and handles a multi-file project better, so long, one-shot requests work well with it. Gemini stands out for how much it can take in at once: hand it a three-hundred-page PDF or a video and it answers about it. What ChatGPT gives you that the others don't, all in one place: it draws images for your site, runs calculations and hands you finished files, talks and listens by voice, and has Canvas for editing without the text scrolling away. Ask each one for what it's good at, and with this one, never drop the magic phrase.

What you paste leaves your computer, and some things can't be unpasted. An API key that shows up in a conversation should be considered burned and changed. A client's data pasted with "Improve the model for everyone" turned on isn't recovered by deleting the conversation afterward, because deletion only affects what happens from that point on, it doesn't rewind. And if your site ends up published with a key written inside the file, anyone who looks at the page's code sees it. Check for this before publishing, not after.
ignore: The model race and its names. Every few weeks a new one comes out with a higher number and gorgeous comparison charts, and half the internet argues over which wins. You only need two: the fast one for writing and the thinking one for code. Knowing how to ask well transfers entirely to the next model; the charts expire in a month.

The GPT store and the hundreds of assistants people have published. It sounds like a shortcut and almost never is: most are mediocre custom instructions with a nice icon. Your own instructions, written by you with your project in them, outperform any of them from day one.

Anything that smells like real-programmer territory: the API, keys, agents that work on your code on their own, and creativity controls. They exist, they're powerful, and they're not for you right now. You'll come back to them the day you have something working and want to automate it; opening that door early only adds screens you don't understand and bills you didn't expect.
